title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
The Aurora ransomware group used Cursor Agent, an AI coding and automation tool running Claude Sonnet, to carry out hands-on exploitation attacks against multiple organizations. The AI tool was not circumvented in a technical sense, it was simply operated by the attackers as a capable assistant for conducting intrusions, the same way a legitimate user would employ it for development tasks. The failure here is one of use-case boundary: the tool was deployed without controls sufficient to prevent its use in active offensive cyber operations against third parties.

This represents an abuse-of-deployment failure rather than a model generating false information or impersonating a person. The AI system functioned as intended, executing tasks directed by its operator. Catching this kind of misuse at deployment would require behavioral monitoring capable of distinguishing malicious reconnaissance and exploitation workflows from ordinary coding assistance, a distinction that is technically difficult and was not, based on the reporting, in place.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic had specific knowledge of this use, whether any platform-level safeguards were attempted and bypassed, or whether the attackers behind the two identified clusters are the same group.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten organizations between April 8 and May 21, 2026. The ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands. Aurora operates a data leak site and targets organizations across multiple countries.

In a separate finding, researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity with medium confidence, possibly from a different operator. This second group targeted eight victim organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina using different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. Gambit Security provided multiple indicators of compromise, including IP addresses, domains, and file hashes associated with both clusters to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.
